report.headline: Usage projected to settle at the NBA average (20.0%), down from a +1.10 sd usage share in the G League, while the efficiency projection carries no signal because the model loses to a trivial baseline on that metric.

projection.text: Usage rate is projected at 20.0% in the NBA, matching the league average of 20.0% exactly, down from a G League usage rate of 25.0% that sat +1.10 sd above that league's mean.

risks.text: Usage is projected to fall from 25.0% to 20.0%, a drop to exactly the NBA average, meaning a smaller share of offensive responsibility than held in the G League.
A 16.7% turnover rate in the source season is a potential concern if ballhandling responsibilities carry over even at reduced usage.
The true shooting projection (52.3%, 80% interval 46.5%–58.2%) comes from a model that does not beat a simple league-average baseline (4.7% error each), so no reliable efficiency read is available.
The estimate rests on only 45 historical GL->NBA transitions, a thin cohort for this move type.

strengths.text: Assist rate of 23.4% and 4.993 assists per 75 possessions point to a significant playmaking role in the source season.
Source-season usage of 25.0% stood +1.10 sd above the G League average, indicating a primary offensive role.
True shooting of 57.4% was +0.33 sd above the G League average, suggesting efficient scoring alongside heavy usage.
34.7% of shot attempts came from three, a profile consistent with floor spacing.

uncertainty.text: The 80% prediction interval for usage runs from 14.7% to 25.3% and the 95% interval from 11.9% to 28.1%, a spread of roughly two league standard deviations (sd = 5.3%), so the model can rank this player against peers but cannot pin down an individual value; on true shooting, the model's held-out error (4.7%) is no better than the best trivial baseline (4.7%), so the 52.3% true shooting projection should not be read as informative.
